headline: Partner @ PwC | Investigations & Forensics
about:
Katrina is a Partner in PwC's Cyber, Risk & Regulatory platform with a focus on investigations and forensics.  She serves as the platform leader for PwC's Consumer Markets Industry, which includes Retail, CPG, Travel, Transportation, and Hospitality clients. She is a Certified Public Accountant and has more than 18 years of financial and business consulting experience. She specializes in providing financial, accounting, economic and business consulting expertise to clients globally. Katrina focuses on helping clients prevent, confront and remediate regulatory, legal and commercial challenges that arise as a result of unplanned events. She has considerable expertise leading and directing clients and teams through large, complicated crisis situations in addition to proactively identifying strategic threats to reduce the risk of future challenges.

Katrina intertwines exceptional project management capabilities with an ability to truly understand the critical issues and specialized subject matter. As such, she has substantial experience managing investigations with multiple, diversified work streams and teams of up to 200 members.

Katrina's forensic and investigative experience includes assignments involving accounting and fraud investigations, cyber security and data breach assistance, Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and anti-corruption compliance assessments, compliance investigations, post-merger/acquisition disputes, licensing management and contract compliance matters, insurance claims, market research and damages analyses. She has provided services to clients in a number of different industries including, but not limited to, healthcare, technology, pharmaceutical and life sciences, insurance, manufacturing, financial services, retail & consumer, construction, entertainment, education, technology, hospitality and gaming.

Katrina has extensive international client and case experiences within the following geographies: Asia, Central Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America and North America.

publications.title: Business ethics: a view from the trenches
publications.description: This article presents results from a study of how young managers define ethical issues, think about these issues, and resolve them. Several patterns emerge from this study. First, in many cases, young managers received explicit instructions from their middle-manager bosses or felt strong organizational pressures to do things that they believed were sleazy, unethical, or sometimes illegal. Second, corporate ethics programs-codes of conduct, mission statements, hot lines, and so forth-proved to be of little help to these young managers. Third, many of them believed that their companies' executives were out-of-touch on ethical issues, either because they were too busy or because they sought to avoid responsibility. Fourth, the young managers resolved the dilemmas they faced largely on the basis of personal reflection and individual values, not through reliance on corporate credos, company loyalty, the exhortations and examples of senior executives, or philosophical principles or religious reflection. Ironically, however, while the interviewees typically described their experiences as difficult or even traumatic, many believed they had learned important lessons about themselves and the world of work.

publications.title: Support for IFRS in Microsoft Dynamics 365: Leveraging D365 to reduce risk and improve control efficiency
publications.description:
In order to maintain consistency and comparability of reporting financial results of global organizations, International Reporting Standards (IFRS) have been designed and implemented across the world as a standard format for companies to report their financial results in an easily understandable and comparable nature.  The globalization of business and finance has led to the mass adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).  

Technology is a key enabler for addressing the change and complexity in an organization’s compliance environment. It’s crucial that you understand how your underlying technology environment can support your business process, compliance, and regulatory requirements such as IFRS and SOX.

Microsoft Dynamics 365 is an enterprise resource planning (ERP) solution for midsize and large organizations that empowers people to work effectively, manage change, and compete globally. Dynamics 365 makes it easy to operate across locations and countries/regions by standardizing processes, providing visibility across your organization, and helping simplify compliance.

Although the dimensions of IFRS and SOX are far-reaching and can be complicated, Dynamics 365 has been designed to include capabilities that help organizations meet their compliance obligations in a flexible, adaptable, and scalable fashion.

PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Microsoft developed a white paper together to explain how Microsoft Dynamics AX can help organizations appropriately use and apply the IFRS standard.

PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Microsoft - Publication date - July, 2021

publications.title: Mitigating Compliance Risk with Dynamics 365 Finance
publications.description:
The US regulatory environment is continually changing, and organizations must maintain awareness of the legal, regulatory and capital impacts of their business decisions. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to restore and enhance public confidence in the financial reporting and disclosure process and improve executive responsibility and accountability.

Many organizations face compliance concern related to Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX). This rule requires management to assess the effectiveness of the company's internal control over financial reporting, including the appropriateness of the control documentation, and report on internal controls within an organization’s annual report to shareholders. Organizations that maintain a deliberate SOX compliance strategy are more likely to strike the right balance between compliance adoption, organizational agility, and growth. 

Technology is a key enabler to address the change and complexity in an organization’s compliance environment. It is crucial to understand how your underlying technology environment can help support your business process, compliance and regulatory requirements such as Sarbanes-Oxley.
 
While the compliance obligations of Sarbanes-Oxley are broad and can be complicated, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance includes functionality that helps organizations meet their compliance obligations in a flexible, adaptable, and scalable fashion. 

This whitepaper discusses the dimensions of SOX and some relevant aspects of Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance to help customers address SOX compliance.

PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Microsoft - Publication date - July, 2021

publications.title: Microsoft Dynamics 365 - Considerations When Adopting One Version
publications.description:
Microsoft has introduced a new approach to updating their Dynamics 365 for Finance and Operations SaaS solution that incorporates all updates into a service update cycle called One Version. One Version introduces a solution to the Microsoft Dynamics 365 for Finance and Operations SaaS update model to give customers the opportunity to update their environment with the latest hotfixes, improvements, and new functionality. 

Frequent updates require attention to prevent the risk that your controls framework is impacted. Most regulations (e.g., SoX, GxP) allow for a risk-based approach to be taken when dealing with system changes. This means the company is responsible for confirming the requirements of their regulations. The question to be asked is, “How can my organization effectively utilize the features and functionality of a SaaS Dynamics 365 for Finance and Operations environment, all while minimizing risk, to implement an efficient, focused process to validate all updates going into my environment?”

To meet compliance requirements for different regulations, customers going through a regular update cycle for their Dynamics 365 for Finance and Operations environment should apply a set of considerations to their update cycle. While each customer’s environment is unique, the following are core considerations that Dynamics 365 for Finance and Operations customers are responsible for:
1) Change Policies and Procedures
2) Impact Assessment
3) Risk Assessment
4) Customization / Extensions
5) Evaluation of Functionality (Positive Testing)
6) Evaluation of Functionality (Negative Testing)
7) Evaluation of Intenal Controls
8) Evaluation of End-to-End Impact (Regression)
9) Security: Using the impact assessment and risk assessment

PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Microsoft developed a white paper together to help organizations consider their compliance responsibilities around the updated approach.  

PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Microsoft - Publication date - June 2019

headline: Audit Partner at PwC Chicago
about:
I am an experienced audit professional and partner at PwC where I have spent my entire career to date. Over my career I have worked with clients in a variety of industries including professional services, technology and industrial products and have focused mostly and most recently on public companies (often multinational) in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector. I regularly work with clients through accounting and auditing matters related to difficult and complex events and transactions including public offerings, acquisitions, carve-outs and spin-offs, implementation of internal controls, restructuring activities, impairments and going concern.

People are my passion - my clients and my PwC colleagues. I enjoy working with, learning from, supporting and helping clients and professionals achieve their goals and realize their potential. I am strong advocate and promoter of inclusion in the workplace and world; a believer that opportunity for all makes us all better. I challenge myself and my teams to deliver value to our clients through the audit and innovation in everything that we do.

I enjoy good food and drink, traveling, laughing regularly and physical activities (what it's called when I do it) / sports (the proper term; what I watch). I am a blessed husband and father to three amazing kids, proud Illinois alum and avid Chicago sports fan.

experience.description:

I currently serve clients in our Pharmaceutical and Life Sciences and Industrial Products practices.  Also have had recent experience serving clients in our Technology practice.

My recent client experiences have primarily focused on accounting for business combinations, collaboration and licensing arrangements, revenue recognition, carve-out audits and impairment reviews at high growth companies. I also have extensive experience serving as the lead manager on large, multinational public companies.  I have had significant training and experience with Sarbanes-Oxley implementation and compliance, fraud risk and controls, and SEC reporting

volunteering.description:
Volunteer & Member Board of Trustees - La Rabida Children’s Hospital mission is simple: they are dedicated to maintaining and improving the quality of life for each patient with complex conditions, disabilities, and chronic illness. The path to completing this mission, however, is often complicated. Patients regularly require extensive care coordination or assistance in managing lifelong conditions. Fortunately, they’ve got the best team around.
They've assembled a care staff of the best, most highly experienced physicians and providers in Chicago. Through relationships with University of Chicago Comer Children’s Hospital, Lurie Children’s Hospital and others, we ensure our patients have the gold-standard of healthcare.
Each child and family in their care is assigned a case manager or care coordinator to oversee treatment and provide 24/7 support. Illnesses don’t work 9-to-5, so neither do they. They pride themselves on being your partner and guide through treatment, day or night, so that children at their centers can return home as soon as medically possible.
We firmly believe that every child deserves care, regardless of a family’s ability to pay (more than 90% of our patients are insured through Medicare). The only thing a kid should worry about is being a kid. Your child is the center of your world — and the center of ours.

about:
Hi, everyone! I'm glad you're here. 

People come to me for all things Organizational Change Management. I drive training content development, communications development, change impacts analyses, change agent network meetings, and project management.

My North Star throughout my time at PwC is my psychology-backed humanistic approach to client obsession. When client collaborators and stakeholders are given the autonomy to make the change journey their own, are given the resources and tools necessary to demonstrate their competence, and are communicated with as if they are part of a community, their working psychological needs have been met and change adoption is achievable.

headline: PwC Deals Partner
about:
Nitin is a Deals partner with over 20 years of experience in leading large scale transformative divestitures starting from strategy phase through post deal optimization. As a part of the Divestiture engagements, Nitin is focused on leveraging fundamental learnings from the Deal Strategy and Diligence phases to inform downstream operational cross-functional separation complexities. Nitin has significant experience running divestitures with global footprint, and deep knowledge in specific divestiture topics like Legal Entity Separation, Operating Models, Physical/Logical Separation, Transition Services Agreements, Public Company Readiness, etc. 

Nitin has helped his clients to develop a 'value based approach' across the divestiture continuum to track the deal's performance with factual data and provides opportunities to maximize on the three components of deal's value:
(+) Deal Strategy: Proactive identification of the gap between intrinsic value and value based on recent multiples allows for tangible opportunities to narrow the gap and capture value
(+) Transition Costs: Effective and proactive management of the costs to do a Divestiture (One-time separation costs, NewCo Stand-up Costs, and Stranded Costs)
(+) Seller/ParentCo Optimization: Divestitures provide a unique opportunity to optimize / resize remaining business

In addition, over the past decade, Nitin has been at the forefront of digitizing PwC's Divestiture Services by embedding more technology and advanced data analytics solutions.

publications.title: Driving digital innovation while managing risk
publications.description:
How can organizations think and act to create a strategic, robust data roadmap and manage related risks?

There’s no question that data analytics innovations, artificial intelligence and machine learning models create new data-driven business opportunities and value. But these trends complicate the risk discussion.

Simply put, more data use incurs more risk: from failing to meet changing market expectations, to addressing evolving public policy requirements and privacy issues, to challenges to internal decision-making processes. This could eventually lead to new data governance laws and regulations, like the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation, or leave value on the table due to ineffective
data use decision-making.

Watch this recorded webcast where a panel of our digital and privacy specialists led by David Sapin, US Advisory Risk & Regulatory Consulting Leader discuss:

- How companies may mitigate these risks with their need to do more with data, balancing
innovation with risk

- How these data challenges may drive internal governance and influence public policy

- How organizations may enable roles charged with data monetization strategies to better
address these issues

- As companies create, acquire and use more data, how they can develop a more holistic,
integrated and flexible data risk profile

publications.title: Next Generation Architecture
publications.description:
Lessons from the Front Line of Implementing Successful Big Data Strategies

C-suite executives overwhelmingly prioritize that the greatest source of value creation for their enterprises over the next decade will come from better utilizing their information and analytics; but then in almost the next sentence, they state that they don't have a big data strategy or blueprint for transforming their organizations. IT infrastructures and applications around big data have arguably outpaced organizations’ ability to realize large scale benefits.

This seminar will help companies plan and implement big data initiatives, including:
- Guidance on ‘art of the possible’ and how to scope opportunities from consultants and executives who have successfully implemented big data driven innovation
- A look at how to build an information strategy that focuses on understanding business ‘wants and needs’ and connecting them to the required organization capabilities
- Panels and expert presentations on how to evaluate big data applications and to see through all the vendor hype that exists in this crowded marketplace

publications.title: A climatic tipping point: environmental disclosure goes mainstream
publications.description:
Almost two decades ago, CDP’s founders believed shareholders needed access to corporate environmental data to make sound investment decisions. In 2015, while the world was focused on the upcoming COP 21 that ultimately would lead to the Paris Agreement, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) quietly launched the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The FSB asked the TCFD to understand how climate change would affect global markets, and what information companies needed to disclose to the investment community to assess climate-related risk and opportunity. 

Given the shared objectives of TCFD and CDP, it comes as no surprise that the latter fully has integrated the TCFD recommendations into the 2018 CDP questionnaires, including a focus on sector-specific questions. As companies prepare for the 2018 CDP cycle, they should ensure their climate change management approach adheres to these changing disclosure expectations.

publications.description:
Back in 2011, one of the world's largest certified Global Reporting Initiative trainings to date took place in Cleveland, drawing nearly 200 business students and college seniors from 14 colleges in Ohio.

The event, held at Cleveland State University and hosted by consultancy BrownFlynn, revolved around a theme that has grown in importance since then: Developing sustainability capacity within a geographic region.

Around the country, cohorts of cities and various regional allies are tackling sustainability through a variety of mechanisms.

The Pittsburgh region exemplifies one strategic approach to regionally tackling sustainability issues.

This includes advising on the accounting and financial reporting implications that arise during these complex transactions. Ethan ensures that clients have a comprehensive understanding of the financial aspects involved, allowing them to make informed decisions and meet regulatory requirements.

about:
As a Partner at PwC, I have over three decades of experience in advising companies ranging from pre-IPO to Fortune 500, on strategic, operational, financial, tax, and governance matters—with a focus on global companies undergoing business transformation, either digitally or through M&A.

My role has enabled me to work with members of the C-Suite, Boards, and various committees on financial reporting, auditing, technology, regulatory, and governance matters. Over my tenure, I have advised some of the Firm’s largest clients through times of immense change and crisis. 

As a senior Partner at PwC and the Firm’s first female Vice Chair, I have been proud to serve marquis clients within Consumer Markets and across numerous industries around the world, as both a senior relationship partner and global lead tax partner. One of my greatest passions is working with clients, learning about their business, and delivering leading-edge expertise that enables them to realize their strategic vision and thrive in a changing world. 

As a trusted advisor, I provide clients a global perspective on risk, technology, and value chain transformation, offering a broad lens on the most critical issues impacting Consumer Markets organizations today across supply chain, distribution, tariffs, innovation, shifting consumer behaviors, scenario planning, and more.  

Currently serving on the boards and committees of Hadley (Chair, Audit Chair), The Chicago Network (Programming Chair, Board Member) and NRF Foundation (Board Member). Formerly served on Dean’s Council for the University of Illinois Gies College of Business (Member). 

I am a proud mom of two daughters, with a passion for advancing professionals in the firm and the greater business community to pave the way for our next generation of leaders. It has been my honor to be recognized by many prestigious organizations including Crain’s 2024 Notable Leaders in Accounting, Consulting & Law, Crain’s 2019 & 2020 Notable Woman Executives Over 50, North Shore Women In Businesswomen’s Leadership Award, Power 50 Award from the Illinois National Diversity Council, and a participant of the CEO Perspectives Leadership Program.

An active runner, I have run the Chicago Marathon twice with my daughter.

Serving clients in the consumer-packaged goods, retail, transportation & logistics, travel, and hospitality sectors, I provide a broad global lens on risk, technology, and value chain transformation with insight on the most critical issues impacting companies today across supply chain, distribution, product innovation, shifting consumer behaviors, and tariffs.

slides.title: Championing inclusive leadership and enhancing employee experience: Insights from my 35-Year career journey
slides.subtitle: Barbra Bukovac on LinkedIn
slides.description: Recently, I had the privilege of sharing my career journey and discussing inclusive leadership at the iConverge 2024 conference hosted by my alma mater, the Gies College of Business - University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign It was an honor to join the stage with distinguished colleagues like Steven Hunter , Global Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion at McDonald's Corporation, and Ann Marie Wright , U.S. Chief Risk Officer at BMO, moderated by of Sean Garrick , Vice Chancellor for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. It was inspiring to feel the energy and enthusiasm from the students and fellow professionals, and I’d like to share some of the key thoughts shared during that session. I started my journey with PwC 35 years ago in the audit and tax practice in Chicago and am proud to be celebrating my 25th year as a partner! What I’ve loved most about my job is the diversity of experiences and learning. I help leading organizations with issues they are struggling with most. I am able to mentor and develop others, particularly women, on their own career paths. And finally, I’ve been able to travel and see the world visiting my clients as they are growing their own businesses in places such as China, India and Europe — while also having the opportunity to interact with my own community, expand my global acumen and have some fun along the way. Career path and leadership style: My career path has been quite a journey. I started fresh out of the undergrad accounting program at the Univ. of IL with the audit group of Price Waterhouse Chicago, then shortly afterwards moved into the firm’s tax practice with a particular focus on international clients. I left the firm for a short period, joining the tax group of one of my Chicago area clients, where I instinctively assumed I'd have a better shot at balancing career aspirations with future family commitments. Looking back at that time in my late twenties, I naively made a significant career decision to leave Price Waterhouse without fully considering what might be possible if I remained at the firm. Fortuitously, I found myself back at PwC. My eyes were open to the opportunities to manage both professional and personal responsibilities where I embraced direct communication and flexibility. I also began to appreciate the importance of direct and open communication with my co-workers and partners, and flexibility in managing both professional and personal responsibilities. Adapting to evolving technologies has streamlined tasks, enabling me to focus on complex analyses and fostering client relationships while developing others. Promoted to Vice Chair eight years ago, I continue to prioritize inclusive leadership, empathy, open communication, and support for team members. Baking inclusion into teams and the workplace: As senior leadership sets the tone for their organization on strategy, they should provide a clear commitment to embedding inclusion into teams and in the workplace. This involves setting measurable goals, providing training on unconscious bias, and fostering open dialogue about inclusion. Encouraging diverse team compositions and ensuring that all voices are heard and valued in meetings and decision-making processes are also crucial. It’s about building a culture where inclusion is part of the everyday fabric of the organization and not a separate program on the side. And at PwC, we don’t sell products — it’s a people and relationship business — so one of the main ways that we embed inclusion into our teams is through the employee experience. Our goal is to provide: An Inclusive culture that promotes community, collaboration, inclusion and belonging Meaningful work, that is purposeful and impactful Holistic support in promoting employee well-being to thrive inside and outside the workplace An adaptive ecosystem such that the technology, workspace and workplace make it easy to do great work at any time, in any place or on any device securely.   We also use technology to help us embed inclusion. For example, we're continuously upskilling our employees by investing in training programs that help our people stay current and prepared for what lies ahead. Educating our people in AI and other emerging technologies not only supports individual growth and opportunity within our organization, but also makes our teams well-equipped to collaborate effectively, regardless of their backgrounds or locations. As we move forward from the insights shared at iConverge 2024, let’s continue to empower and support one another in our diverse career journeys, ensuring that every professional environment champions inclusivity and growth. You can read more about fostering an inclusive culture and how that enhances the employee experience here. slides.title: Women leaders step up to the challenge of creating a more inclusive future
slides.subtitle: Barbra Bukovac on LinkedIn
slides.description: The popular saying about the month of March is that it comes “in like a lion, out like a lamb”. It refers to the often chaotic fluctuations in weather from winter to spring. Many basketball fans also embrace the chaos or “madness” of basketball tournaments in March where teams come into the games on top but where upsets are what keeps everyone buzzing. This year, the elite college athletes and teams experienced and rose to the challenges of performing during the pandemic. However, one of the main stories that unfolded was the inequities between the men’s and women’s tournament -- training conditions and other disparities about the quality of food, gift bags and coronavirus testing also came to light --- disheartening to see amidst so many celebratory stories of women during Women’s History month. I’m a proud mom of two daughters who were both recruited athletes. My oldest daughter played soccer during her four years at her college and served as co-captain and my youngest daughter rowed for her university for two years. I can relate to the supportive parents and hard-working players at the women’s tournament and feel for them. They have trained to be at the top of their game - and when they get their chance to be in the spotlight - they find themselves on an uneven playing field when compared to their male counterparts. A situation that also happens with women leaders in business. We’ve become familiar with the term, “glass ceiling” as an unofficial barrier to advancement that especially affects women and racially/ethnically diverse people. Similarly, the “glass cliff” describes the idea that when a company is in trouble or during particularly challenging circumstances, a female leader is often put in charge and faces greater risk for failure. During the pandemic, stories have been shared that have shown women leaders stepping up to the challenges and leading strongly. The Harvard Business Review completed research that shows women were rated as more effective leaders both before and during the pandemic crisis. While women ranked higher in 13 of the 19 competencies measured, we see some of the largest leads were in taking initiative, inspiring and motivating others, championing change and displaying high integrity and honesty. Women leaders also received higher levels of engagement from their employees during the disruptive work experience. Yet, many articles and studies have shown that women have been hit the hardest during the pandemic. The responsibilities of women have grown as they need to spend more time taking care of their families from young school-age children to older parents and relatives at greater risk. It is no wonder female directors on corporate boards prioritize the importance of cultural and societal issues more strongly than their male counterparts. PwC’s recent corporate directors survey shows significant gender differences in the way female and male directors prioritize such issues as ESG (environmental, social and governance initiatives), human rights and diversity and inclusion. Here are some of the findings: More women directors agree these topics should be incorporated into company strategy: ESG overall - 60% of female directors vs. 46% of male directors Human rights - 79% of female directors vs. 64% of male directors Social movements - 69% of female directors vs. 40% of male directors Incentive plan metrics tied to diversity and inclusion - 58% female directors vs. 32% male directors These results show that expectations are on the rise for companies to demonstrate that their purpose is not just words, but actions that can benefit their stakeholders. Focusing on ESG is key to creating a purpose-driven organization. While ESG is broad, the focus helps build trust with stakeholders and can include topics like developing an inclusive culture that can lead to sustainable long-term growth for a company. Legislators, investors, and other stakeholders are increasingly demanding more diverse boards and it’s even being required. Some financial services organizations are including language about the requirement and several states are starting to introduce it following California’s law which also highlights greater diversity for underrepresented communities. With more female and diverse directors on boards and more diversity in the C-suite, the focus and direction of companies changes. Women leaders have the opportunity and ability to influence companies to make progress on important cultural and societal issues such as diversity and inclusion. And while this change is needed and seen as important, it hasn’t been easy to make it happen. Resources and opportunities haven’t been the same. The women leaders I know have achieved their positions through not only hard work, but also by seeking out specific leadership programs for women, by working with and being supported by advocates and sponsors and by building their network. I encourage women to use their strengths to lead and create inclusive teams to bring different perspectives, creative thinking and open collaboration. A diverse workforce and deliberate inclusion efforts help drive better outcomes that can actually lead to the broader economic development of our society, which benefits everyone. As we see March and Women’s History month come to a close, I feel hopeful and excited to see that spring is here and inspired that the role of women leaders and women’s performance continues to be highlighted, is intentionally supported and begins to expand.

slides.title: How has my experience with technology changed at PwC in the last 30 years? - An interview with my daughter
slides.subtitle: Barbra Bukovac on LinkedIn
slides.description: Recently, my daughter Nicki, a second semester senior at Cornell University, asked to interview me for a school project on technological changes and its impact on my work at PwC during the last 30 years. In a year where work and school have relied more than ever on modern technology, I was happy to reflect on how technology has enabled more efficiency, accuracy and unlocked deeper insights in the accounting, advisory and tax professions over the years. And while technology has impacted and will continue to impact all jobs and careers as we look forward, there is no substitute for human connection and the relationships we build over time. Thanks Nicki and the students at Cornell University for being interested in my career journey as you begin to plan yours. NB: Why did you choose accounting? BB: As you know, my parents both worked for the University of Illinois and they suggested a major in accounting since it was viewed by many as the language of business and a popular major for business students. Going into the fall of my senior year, I had already secured an offer from PwC. I began my career by manually “ticking and tying” numbers from one source document to another in order to audit the accuracy of my client’s financial statements. The majority of my time was spent calculating and recalculating numbers by hand using a “ten-key” adding machine, reviewing and researching volumes of Federal and State tax revenue codes/regulations and other reference books, sorting through and organizing “work papers,” and sending big trunks of physical documents to and from clients. Needless to say, the time it took to perform all these tasks was significant. NB: When did technology start to become a bigger part of the workforce and your job as a whole and how did it change your daily activities? BB: The advent and widespread adoption of new technologies like the internet, cell phones, and personal computers, was a turning point for the profession. It was a really big deal to be able to communicate more quickly and directly with colleagues and clients, and that started to change many aspects of our daily work practices. There’s really no physical documentation anymore because all of our documents are now electronic and kept online, enabling us to share and to move deliverables much more easily. We used to research tax issues in publications and manuals - the firm even had its own in-house office library Before the internet the research process was very cumbersome. Being able to quickly come up with our conclusions on research, and of course how we would communicate our findings to the client on a regular basis, wasn't efficient because we didn't have the internet to help us. Plus, the physical sorting of data and supporting documents as well as recreating and manually recalculating client financial schedules, meant confirming results of an audit or tax project took months and thousands of manhours crammed into late nights and long weekends. NB: While PwC has seen a lot of technology changes in previous decades - how is it staying ahead of all the technology advancements today? BB: PwC has created an environment where its partners and employees embrace the use of technology. In 2016, PwC announced its intention to spend $3 billion dollars on upskilling its employees, specifically surrounding technology. This was not only a program for our client-service professionals but also for our infrastructure personnel and anyone who works at PwC regardless of role or tenure. PwC’s goal was to empower its employees by harnessing technology and use it as a way to help improve each individual’s work experience. The initial upskilling program has been followed up with PwC’s employees undergoing a regular “digital fitness assessment” so that each individual has an idea of how well they understand and utilize the latest technologies and what the best medium is for them to further develop their skills. This program has been a truly innovative approach enabling PwC to invest in its employees while aggressively incorporating the latest technology into the workforce. PwC felt well prepared to have its employees work from home during the COVID-19 pandemic. It really paid off for us during the pandemic because everybody was already comfortable using the technology in their day-to-day work. Our clients have been very happy with our work and we really haven't skipped a beat. NB: So using the technology helped with your own personal development and all of PwC’s. Do you find your clients need education on these platforms too? BB: Over time, our clients’ need for broader types of advice (e.g., technology platforms & implementation to strategic decision making) drove our firm to build and grow large consulting practices which have now become a much more prevalent part of their business. Consulting projects account for over half of PwC’s business today, so we really have dramatically evolved the mix of our business. It’s a result of what our client’s need from us (sophisticated advice to operate on a global stage) and the decline of historical data/fact checking and tax preparation/filing as technology advances continue. We have many clients that are going through transformations of their own business right now, and specifically digital transformations. NB: How has adopting new technology most impacted your career and how do you see it impacting current students about to enter the workforce? BB: Today, employees can spend more time on higher level analyses, develop a deeper understanding of client needs, and focus on building long-term relationships with customers. Without the increase in technology, I wouldn’t be in the role I am today, connecting with clients, facilitating negotiations and building a strong network. These relationships have contributed greatly to the success of the firm and meeting clients' needs. By increasing adoptions of technology, I was enabled to reach a higher level of success as a businesswoman. Today’s workforce and current students have a tremendous opportunity in front of them to embrace technology. Access to data to help make decisions, automation that can increase the speed and accuracy of delivery, and new connectivity and communication methods can lead to great productivity and efficiency. However, one thing that hasn’t changed in the last 30 years is the fact that relationships matter. Fostering personal relationships with colleagues and clients, with and without technology, is what helps bring work success and satisfaction.

slides.title: Women Leadership In Unprecedented Times: A Conversation with PwC’s Central and Midwest Leaders
slides.subtitle: Barbra Bukovac on LinkedIn
slides.description: As PwC’s regional vice chair of the Mid-Central market, I am thrilled to work with the incredible women leading these markets: Carina Markel, newly-named Managing Partner of PwC’s Central Market and Melissa Wasson, our Midwest Market Managing Partner. Our firm recently released its first Diversity and Inclusion Transparency report, and the three of us came together to discuss what’s changed for our people, our clients, and our leadership across our markets in 2020. Barb: Carina, congratulations on being named the new Central Market Managing Partner. It’s quite a time to be taking on this leadership position. How has the current environment impacted the way you approach your new role? Carina: Technology has been key in helping me connect with our people and clients remotely. Our firm had already committed to investing over $3 billion globally to provide our people with the skills and tools to help them thrive in a digital workplace, and we are helping our clients accelerate their digital strategies. Those businesses that succeed and those that will have to play catch-up will be defined by those that transform digitally. Barb: Melissa, you have led the Midwest market for a year now. How have you responded to the changes since the pandemic? Melissa: I’ve learned so much in the last year and one thing that has changed tremendously is communication. We’re leveraging technology to host large market webcasts, sending more frequent email communications and connecting virtually with people one-on-one. I have had the chance to get to know several of our new hires, interns, and new partners across the 11 cities in our market all through video calls, which wasn’t the norm just six months ago. Barb: What are you hearing from clients and what are their biggest priorities heading into 2021? Carina: Navigating the economic fallout resulting from the pandemic has been top of mind for our clients, with 95% of executives saying some type of policy action is needed for the US economy to recover from the effects of the pandemic. In our current environment, hesitation is not an option. Companies that are bold and refocus their strategies now will likely come out stronger and be well-positioned after the pandemic. Melissa: In light of the recent social unrest that has impacted our nation, our clients are challenged to focus on workplace culture ensuring it embraces diversity and prioritizes inclusion. I’m inspired by the response of the business community, and we’ve had many CEOs sign on to CEO Action, the largest coalition of CEOs committed to building productive, diverse and inclusive workplaces. And we know there is much more work to be done. Carina: It’s also important to check in on each other right now. I was in a meeting with one of my clients, who is a Black senior executive, during the start of the protests following George Floyd’s death. Afterward, I reached out to him to ask how he was doing. He opened up that he was really affected by everything that was happening. I appreciated how candid he was and it reemphasized for me the need to take personal interest and care with others and ourselves at work and at home - especially as these lines are more blurred today than ever before. Barb: Absolutely, Carina. As leaders, it is more important than ever that we check in with our teams and encourage our people to connect with each other. Melissa, you hosted a series of ‘Stronger Together’ conversations in your market earlier this summer focusing on race, a subject that can be difficult in any format. How was the response? Melissa: As Carina shared in her interaction with her client, many of our employees have been and continue to be deeply affected by the unrest happening across the country. We hosted a webcast where we had several Black and Latinx employees, as well as allies, share their personal stories. The experiences shared were emotional. So many people wanted to join the conversation that we added another session. After those calls many people reached out to tell me they appreciated having the forum to have conversations with others across our market and felt closer to their colleagues as a result. Barb: Those sessions were very powerful and help our employees speak freely about their own journeys in their personal lives and their careers. PwC’s journey in advancing Diversity and Inclusion in our firm has led us to release our first-ever Diversity and Inclusion Transparency report. As a woman in the workplace, I experienced this flexibility more than 20 years ago when I had the opportunity to work an 80% schedule and spend time at home with my two young daughters. Flexibility, programs, and sponsorship are just a few of the ways the firm is helping our people at the firm continue to grow their careers at the firm and take care of themselves and families. Can you share a little about your journey? Carina: I was born and raised on a commercial pineapple farm in the Philippines, and came to this country on my own to attend college in Ohio. I became the first in my family to immigrate to the United States. Since joining the firm 30 years ago, I've gained opportunities and experiences made possible by leaders who were committed to building and coaching a team and growing our business so that someone like me could build a career in this firm. I am humbled to be the first woman and person of color to lead the Central market and I’m delighted to help drive value to our clients, give back to our communities and most importantly to be able to mentor and create opportunities for others, including my daughter. Melissa: I feel fortunate to be supported as a mother and female leader at the firm. It’s important to have our leaders connect with our partners and teams to bring an empathetic leadership style to every interaction. When we have diversity at the top levels of an organization, it provides diversity of perspective for our people. Barb: You’re absolutely right -- advancing our representation starts at the top. PwC has one of the most diverse leadership teams in corporate America. We are committed to achieving global gender equality in the workplace and beyond, and both of you are a representation of that. I appreciate both of you for taking time to share with me your stories today and for all the work you are doing for our people in our Mid-Central region.

headline: Senior Manager at PwC
about:
I am currently a Senior Manager at PricewaterhouseCoopers. I'm a driven, hard-working leader that works well in a group environment.  My time at PwC has exposed me to dynamic and ever-changing opportunities that show my ability to think on my feet to help our clients overcome challenges. My particular focus is in our Banking Capital Markets group, with clients ranging from broker dealers, commercial banks to middle market direct lending firms.

I'm also a graduate of the University of Notre Dame, where I earned my bachelor's degree in Accounting through the Mendoza College of Business. I was very involved on campus as well during my four years, including participation in the Men's Boxing program and a leader in the Student International Business Council.

experience.description: I am a leader on multiple clients in the banking and capital markets industry, spanning from broker dealers to large commercial banks. My role involves direct interaction with Senior management, including the Board of Directors and Audit Committee, in order to better directly address concerns and challenges they are facing. As a senior member of our audit team, I'm tasked with coaching our junior members, budgeting for the upcoming audit, and ensuring the design of our audit procedures appropriately address the identified risks.

I had been a lead Manager on multiple clients within the broker dealer, commercial banking, and private credit industries. My role involved managing the progress of the audit, coaching other team members, and performing testing over significant risk areas of the audit. This included items such as investment valuation, complex revenue, allowance for credit loss, relevant controls, and debt related testing.
I lead the audit team in carrying out the financial statement audits of several large banking and asset management clients, including broker dealers, private credit, and fund of fund clients.
I worked with large asset management and hedge fund clients on carrying-out their year-end financial statement audits.

I assisted in preparing and carrying-out the 2015 audit for a large investment management client. My role included reviewing test controls and examining significant transactions that occurred throughout the year.

Generate research on new business opportunities and possible new partnerships, created a more efficient system for data collection, and assisted in dramatic company growth over just a few months time.

Owned and operated a food service facility with three of my friends at Notre Dame. Sold specialty food and were open at late hours of the weeknights, serving close to 200 students per week. Throughout the year, we saw substantial revenue growth, due in part to our delivery service and marketing campaigns throughout campus. This experience gave me a feel for running a small business as I assisted in all aspects of operations, including inventory procurement, sales, and assessment of financials. We also chose to donate 10% of all profits to a local charity which assists in child tutoring and development.

Helped with budgeting donations and prepared for an audit, created a Microsoft Excel guide to be distributed around the office as a reference. I also worked with the development team to market the impact that PIH has on global health and how to engage younger generations on joining the movement to a healthier world.

Most recently, I traveled to Rwanda with PIH to visit their hospitals and see how my work impacted local communities. I had the chance to visit patients in their homes to see first hand the poverty that they endure each and every day.

volunteering.description: Traveled down to West Virginia for a week during the summer to help rebuild homes and relieve poverty in some of the poorest areas of the country. Groups help build foundations, re-apply new siding, and finish entire additions to homes. During my time their, I was able to interact with the owners of the homes to gain a better feel for the daily poverty that they endured.

Quinn is a Chicago-based associate in PwC’s Risk & Regulatory practice with a specific focus on the financial services industry. He has experience, primarily in SOX compliance (both IT and business processes), and has worked closely with Internal Audit teams to provide insights and support on controls testing, walkthroughs, and issue remediation efforts in the private equity sector. He has assisted clients with designing and implementing internal controls as well as assessing control design and operating effectiveness during his tenure at PwC.

Quinn has demonstrated the ability to effectively collaborate with and coach both manager-level and peer resources. He works independently with a strong sense of urgency and brings clear ownership to his responsibilities. Quinn is a strong communicator who clearly articulates testing approaches, status, and outcomes to both engagement teams and business stakeholders. He takes direction well, executes independently, and consistently follows up with thoughtful, well-formed questions. Quinn also has experience creating process flowcharts and identifying key risks and controls.

headline: Partner, Deals
about:
Lev Holubec is a Consulting Partner on the Global Senior Leadership Team of PwC’s Deals business. 
Specializing in untangling the complexities of cross-border deals, he has assisted clients across a variety of industries to deliver on their deal value promise.  Lev exudes high, magnetic energy engaging the best of people to develop and deliver efficient bespoke solutions on unique and challenging deals.

He is co-leader, together with his CEE based partner Todd Bradshaw, of PwC's Rebuild Ukraine Global Task Force which aims to bring the best of the firm's capabilities to contribute to the rebuild and evolution of next generation Ukraine.   His primary focus includes building and operationalizing the most effective private sector alliances to accelerate an efficient rebuild, helping investors understand and navigate the reconstruction landscape, and assisting clients on operating in Ukraine.

Globally credentialed, Lev has delivered tangible value to his clients’ bottom line on projects in more than 28 countries on three continents.  From 2008-2012 Lev led PwC’s merger and acquisition integration services across Central and East Europe, from his base in Kyiv, Ukraine. In 2000-2001 he served multinational clients as a Senior Manager on the PwC M&A team in London, England.  Lev sold and designed process control systems for factories with the Reliance Electric Company from 1990-1992, and transitioned to his consulting career in E&Y’s Supply Chain practice from 1994 until 1997 when he joined PwC.

Lev, who is bilingual Ukrainian/English, earned a BS in Physics from John Carroll University and an MBA in Management of Organizations from Columbia University.  He has authored numerous articles and has spoken at U.S. and European conferences on topics related to making deals successful and leveraging an acquisition to transform a business, and Ukraine's reconstruction.

Lev enjoys traveling with his wife Halyna and their eighteen year old, high school senior twins Oresta and Ruslan. He also enjoys running and collects GPS maps of his longer runs in each of the states and countries where he travels for work or pleasure.

- Assessing IPO readiness and evaluating strategic alternatives

publications.title: H1'20 Capital Markets Watch
publications.description:
US IPO market rebounds after months of relative quiet. The IPO market in the first half of 2020 was very much a tale of three parts:

Compared to the second half of 2019, the total number of issuances remained relatively flat, but 2020 proceeds were up more than 50% despite periods of high volatility. Compared to the first half of last year, the first half of 2020 saw only a slight reduction in IPO activity, with the 2020 market pricing seven fewer IPOs and raising 8% less in proceeds.

US IPOs were dominated by issuances from the pharma and life sciences (PLS) and SPACs sectors in H1’20. PLS IPO volume was flat compared to H1’19, with biotech comprising more than 80% of all PLS volume, while PLS proceeds were up 148%.­­

publications.title: The 2020 IPO comeback: What previous rebounds tell us
publications.description:
PwC's Deals Blog publications provide the latest dealmaking perspectives from the firm's specialists.

This article in particular profiles historic IPOs in 2003, 2009, and 2011 that "reopened" the IPO markets to define the profile of a company that might do the same in 2020.  A tsunami of pent-up demand can send that next deal soaring, and the rest of the market coming forth based on a vision of comparability. The question in our minds is not only when, but more importantly, will companies be ready when the market reopens?

publications.title: Myth busting – Going public during election years
publications.description:
As the 2020 presidential election draws closer, companies considering an IPO are increasingly discussing the potential impacts on their plans to go public.  They correctly recognize key company and industry issues intersecting with the regulatory and political environment and worry the election may significantly affect their company’s prospects. Given these forces at play, many market participants have been advising IPO candidates to avoid the second half of 2020. Is this caution warranted? In our view, no. History shows those concerns are overdone. Historical IPO volume has been largely unaffected in previous election years, with the exception of biotech/pharma which has been hurt by political saber-rattling on drug prices.

publications.title: Dual-Track Exit Considerations
publications.description:
During the past several years, owners and companies have increased the use of creative exit strategies to provide themselves additional flexibily. We see companies using a wide variety of strategies - minority interests, joint ventures, Initial Public Offerings (IPO) and outright sales - to monetize their investments. Most commonly, we see a dual track strategy by private equity (PE) sponsors and venture capital firms which involve pursuing an IPO while simultaneously exploring the sale of portfolio companies through a private auction. 

We see variations in how dual-track strategies are executed, depending on factors such as market conditions, sponsor motivations, and resources available. Firms may choose to be proactive or reactive in their approach—either openly pursuing willing buyers while moving closer to an IPO, or only considering purchase offers they receive.

headline: Partner at PwC leading Finance Transformation for our Insurance and Financial Services Clients
about:
“Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it” – Henry David Thoreau

Financial Services clients recognize the need to invest in their finance and accounting organizations, enabling finance to move beyond production, providing the business better analytics and insights to drive the strategy forward. I collaborate with clients to improve their finance operating models, leading to increases in efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, to be successful in my current role as the leader of Finance Transformation in the US Insurance sector, I build teams and collaborate with my colleagues that bring domain expertise in the areas of Cloud and Digital, Actuarial, Investments, Change Management, Accounting, Tax, & Workforce Transformation.   

My clients benefit from almost 30 years of finance and consulting experience. Drawing from a combination of Global and Domestic experience at over 27 Insurers, 3 Insurance Brokers, 7 Diversified Banks, 2 Investment Banks, 2 Insurance Company divestitures, 3 PE-owned Insurance Platforms and the IPO of a Private Equity firm, my clients benefit from perspective and leading practices. Clients appreciate my openness, honesty, flexibility, and the fact that I listen closely.  And I am never afraid to “roll-up my sleeves” and jump in the trenches. Moreover, collaboration leads to practical solutions with realistic timetables and budgets, recognizing every successful transformation or solution requires some level of differentiation when it comes to the approach.

When I am not spending time with my clients, I spend as much time as possible with my wife Jen raising our four boys. We have lived in Chicago since 1994, and are raising our family in the city. My favorite past times are sailing, tennis, skiing, traveling, and enjoying the entertainment and arts offered by the city of Chicago. Our family also likes to explore new places in our RV and spend time at our lake home in Wisconsin. In terms of community service, I volunteer my time as a Coach (see Volunteering) and we are active members in our St. Clement Parish.

I bring expertise in AI/ML including Gen AI applications for financial services, certifications in GARP Risk and AI (RAI), GARP Sustainability and Climate Risk (SCR) and and Human-Centered Design (HCD), which reflect my passion for solving complex risk challenges through quantitative and innovative solutions. As a driven leader, I have established the Risk Analytics Center of Excellence (CoE) at PwC US and Accenture Management Consulting. publications.description:
This second machine age has seen the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), or
“intelligence” that is not the result of human cogitation. It is now ubiquitous
in many commercial products, from search engines to virtual assistants.
AI is the result of exponential growth in computing power, memory capacity,
cloud computing, distributed and parallel processing, open-source solutions,
and global connectivity of both people and machines. The massive amounts
and the speed at which structured and unstructured (e.g., text, audio, video,
sensor) data is being generated has made a necessity of speedily processing
and generating meaningful, actionable insights from it.

headline: Managing Director at PricewaterhouseCoopers
about:
I am a Managing Director in the PwC Financial Markets practice based in Chicago. I focus on providing transaction and valuation services with a focus on real estate valuation, due diligence and consulting. 

I have over 29 years of experience working with clients to understand the value of their real estate.  My experience includes real estate valuation for a variety of purposes specializing in valuation for  financial and tax reporting purposes (such as purchase price allocations, goodwill impairment studies, fresh start accounting, property and estate tax, 861 studies), due diligence studies, corporate real estate consulting, feasibility studies, appraisal management outsourcing, real estate valuation for financing, litigation support, and insurable value studies. 

Prior valuation and consulting assignments have included all types of commercial  property (including, but not limited to, hotel/casino, retail, office, industrial, multi family, rights-of-way, mining/utilities, agriculture, and other specialized uses) spanning industries in local, national and international markets for a variety of clients including financial institutions, real estate funds, REITs, public and private companies, sovereign wealth and private equity funds.

I currently hold MAI and MRICS designations and hold State certified General Appraiser licenses in a number of States.  

Prior to joining PwC in Chicago, I worked as a Director with Duff & Phelps, Standard & Poor's Corporate Value Consulting and a Manager with Arthur Andersen's Real Estate Consulting/Valuation Practice.

projects.title: Data mining application for CH-47D AFT swashplate bearing fault detection
projects.associatedWith: Associated with University of Illinois at Chicago
projects.description:
The project was based on the paper "Inserted fault vibration monitoring tests for a CH-47D AFT swash plate bearing". 
The data consisted of 6 specimens of the CH-47D helicopter swashplate bearing. Each data sheet consisted of 30000 frequency data, for 6 different faults detected in the bearing. 

Aim of the project was the identify the bearing fault based on the given non-classified data. 

1. Wavelet coefficient data was obtained by Fourier transforming vibration data for each specimen.
2. This transformed data, consisting of 120 data points and 255 features was used for the final training of the algorithms.
3. Various methods like Regressive Forward Elimination (RFE), MARS, Random forest and, Boruta methods were used for feature selection. The total number of effective features was reduced to 8.
4. Data mining and machine learning algorithms such as Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors and discriminant analysis was used for the the classification.
5. A final accuracy of 90% was achieved. 
6. The project was compiled using R.

projects.description:
The project was based on a research paper published: Frey, P. W. , and Slate, D. J., 1991, “Letter Recognition using Holland-Style Adaptive Classifiers”, Machine Learning.

The research for this article investigated the ability of several variations of Holland-style adaptive classifier systems to learn to correctly guess the letter categories associated with vectors of 16 integer attributes extracted from raster scan images of the letters.

The aim of the project was to use other classifiers to try to obtain a better result than the one achieved in the paper., using the same data.

1. The data was first sorted and the f-stat of the features was used to select the relevant features.
2. Data Mining classifiers such as K-nearest neighbors, Discriminant analysis, and Naive Bayer's  were used for the classification.
3. An accuracy of 93% was achieved, higher than the accuracy of 80% achieved in the research paper.
4. The project was compiled using XLMiner.

The initial focus of the Subcommittee includes an analysis of the implications for digital technologies firms and digital technologies products and services when using a combination of data, culture, and behavioral science tools to assess risk and map organizational culture impacting that risk in a manner that helps to strengthen, redesign and retool digital technologies' compliance programs.

The New York City Bar Association (City Bar) Presidential Task Force on Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies (Task Force) is composed of more than 200 representatives of more than 50 committees, councils, and other task forces of the City Bar and adjunct members, including lawyers, academics, trade association representatives, consultants, technologists, and others. Virtually every City Bar practice area is represented on the Task Force. The primary mission of the Task Force is to create a Center of Excellence and Thought Leadership in artificial intelligence and digital technologies, including innovative technologies that create new or enhanced products and services, digital assets, and more efficient, convenient, and effective ways of doing business.
